title.source: How did war change daily life in Singapore?

essentialQuestion.source: What can different sources tell us about daily life in a time of war, and what can they not tell us?

learningGoal.source: Describe two ways the Japanese occupation changed daily life in Singapore, using a source for each, and say what a modern photo cannot show.

warmUp.question.source: When food is hard to find, what could change in a school day?

evidence.question.source: Which source tells you about school? Which tells you about food? Which shows the place today?

evidence.cards.0.title.source: Three real sources about Singapore, 1942 to 1945

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.caption.source: Source 1: "The Japanese Occupation", a history page by Singapore's Ministry of Education Heritage Centre (a modern account)

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.0.source: It says education almost stopped from 1942 to 1945, because many schools were destroyed or taken for military use.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.1.source: It says the Japanese military government made the teaching of Japanese compulsory in schools in 1942.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.2.source: It says teachers had to learn Japanese and were not allowed to use English in school.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.3.source: It says that as food ran short, many schools grew their own food, and gardening became part of lessons.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.4.source: Limit: it tells us about rules and examples. It does not tell us what every child did.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.caption.source: Source 2: "Wartime Victuals", an article by Lee Geok Boi for the National Library Board, 2019

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.0.source: It is built from the National Archives of Singapore's oral history interviews, many of them recorded in the 1980s.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.1.source: It says Singapore bought most of its food from other places, and the war cut the ships and trains that brought rice.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.2.source: It says every household had to register to get ration cards, and the rice ration became smaller over time.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.3.source: It says many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice, and school fields became vegetable plots.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.4.source: Limit: memories are valuable, but each one is one person's account, told many years later.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.caption.source: Source 3: A photo of the Former Ford Factory, Bukit Timah, Singapore, taken on 19 September 2025 by Actuall7

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.0.source: It shows the restored factory building, with modern flats behind it.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.1.source: The National Archives of Singapore says British forces surrendered here on 15 February 1942. It now holds an exhibition about the war.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.2.source: Limit: it shows the place in 2025. It cannot show what people ate or learned in 1942.

evidence.cards.1.events.0.text.source: British forces surrender at the Ford Factory. The Japanese occupation begins.

evidence.cards.1.events.1.text.source: Teaching Japanese becomes compulsory in schools.

evidence.cards.1.events.2.text.source: Ration cards, smaller rice rations, tapioca and sweet potatoes, school vegetable plots.

evidence.cards.1.events.4.text.source: The National Archives records oral history interviews about the occupation.

evidence.cards.1.events.5.text.source: Lee Geok Boi's article about wartime food is published.

evidence.cards.1.events.6.text.source: Actuall7 photographs the Former Ford Factory.

read.sections.0.heading.source: A place and a turning point

read.sections.0.text.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This began the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today the factory holds an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, everyday routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost time in class. People did not all live through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us a place. It cannot show us how people lived there in 1942.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces gave up Singapore. Japanese forces took control. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. It lasted until 1945. The British gave up in a factory. Today the building has a show about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children missed school. People had different lives. A photo of the building today shows a place. It does not show how people lived in 1942.

read.sections.1.text.source: Singapore's Ministry of Education Heritage Centre writes about schools in this time. It says the Japanese military government made Japanese lessons compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese, and they could not use English in school. There was a shortage of food, so many schools grew their own. Gardening became part of lessons. Tapioca, a root that grows easily, became an important food. This source tells us about rules and examples of school life. It does not tell us that every child went to school or had the same lessons. For most children, school almost stopped.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A history centre in Singapore writes about schools in this time. It says Japanese lessons were compulsory from 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese. There was a shortage of food. So many schools grew food. Tapioca is a root plant that grows easily. It became an important food. This source shows us rules. It does not show that every child went to school.

read.sections.2.text.source: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut the ships and trains that brought rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for the National Library in 2019. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice. Some food was sold in secret at very high prices, so people with more money could get more. For most people, meals were not enough to stay healthy. To learn about meals then, we need food records or memories, not a photo of the factory now.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Before the war, most food came to Singapore by ship. The war stopped much of the rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about this in 2019. She used oral history. Each home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold in secret, for a lot of money. Most people did not get enough food to stay healthy. The photo of the factory does not show what people ate.

read.glossary.0.definition.source: A time when an army from another country controls a place.

read.glossary.0.example.source: The Japanese occupation of Singapore lasted from 1942 to 1945.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: A recording of a person telling what they remember.

read.glossary.1.example.source: Lee Geok Boi used oral history to learn what people ate in the war.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: Something you must do because it is a rule.

read.glossary.2.example.source: Japanese lessons became compulsory in Singapore's schools in 1942.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: When there is not enough of something that people need.

read.glossary.3.example.source: A shortage of rice meant many people ate tapioca instead.

read.glossary.4.definition.source: A fixed amount of food each person is allowed to get.

read.glossary.4.example.source: In Singapore, the rice ration got smaller as the war went on.

read.checks.0.question.source: In what year did British forces surrender in Singapore?

read.checks.0.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. British forces gave up Singapore in 1942. Then the occupation began.

read.checks.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. 1945 is when the occupation ended. Look at the first date in the first part of the reading.

read.checks.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. 2025 is when the photo of the building was taken. Look at the first part of the reading.

read.checks.1.question.source: The photo of the factory was taken in 2025. What can it show?

read.checks.1.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A photo from 2025 cannot show meals from 1942. Food records or memories could help.

read.checks.1.options.1.text.source: Whether every family had enough food

read.checks.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The photo shows a building, not food. Look at the end of the third part of the reading.

read.checks.1.options.2.text.source: What the building looks like now

read.checks.1.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The photo shows the place in 2025. It is evidence of a place, not of daily life in the war.

write.prompt.source: Write two notes. Give one fact about school or food, and say where it comes from. Then say one thing the 2025 photo cannot show.

write.selfCheck.0.source: I gave one fact about school or food.

write.selfCheck.1.source: I named the source of my fact.

write.selfCheck.2.source: I said one thing the photo cannot show.

write.example.source: One change in school was that Japanese lessons became compulsory in 1942. I know this from the school history centre. One change in food was that many people ate tapioca or sweet potatoes. Rice was hard to get. I know this from Lee Geok Boi's article. She used oral history. The 2025 photo cannot show what one family ate in 1942. It only shows the building today.

speak.partnerTask.source: With a partner, describe two different changes in daily life, one about school and one about food, and name the source for each. Then ask: whose experience is still missing?

speak.independentTask.source: Record or write two sentences: one change in daily life with its source, and one group of people whose memories you would still want to hear.

watch.why.source: In a calm cooking show from Singapore's National Library, Lee Geok Boi explains why people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes in the war, then cooks with them.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: What might people eat when rice is hard to find?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Which two root vegetables does the cook use instead of rice?

watch.summary.source: This video is part of a cooking show from Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, make food from the time of the Japanese occupation. First, they talk about the past. There was a shortage of rice in the war. So people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead. Tapioca was easy to grow. The video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold in secret for a lot of money. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only foods that people could get at the time. She makes noodles from tapioca and sweet potato. She also makes boiled tapioca with coconut. The video says tapioca fills you up, but it does not give the body all it needs to stay healthy.

watch.keyPoints.0.source: During the Japanese occupation, rice was hard to get, so many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes.

watch.keyPoints.1.source: Food was shared out with rations, and some food was sold in secret at high prices.

watch.keyPoints.2.source: Tapioca grows easily and fills you up, but it does not give the body everything it needs.

watch.contentNote.source: Not yet watched by a person. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 1 November 2026; length (18:16) from YouTube's listing. The summary is written only from the video's YouTube description and chapter list and from the National Library's page for it (BiblioAsia, "Tapioca Tales", 14 April 2022), not from watching it or from its captions. It is long: the history part runs from about 1:48 to 5:48, and the rest is cooking, so you can stop early. Preview the chapters "The cookbook written by civilian internees" (3:51) and "Malnourishment among prisoners of war" (5:04): they may show photos of very thin, hungry people. It ends with a section on Total Defence Day (15:25), a Singapore civic campaign. Check for advertising before the video.

visual.alt.source: A timeline from 1942 to 1945. It starts with the British surrender on 15 February 1942 and ends when the occupation ends in 1945. One note shows school changes: compulsory Japanese lessons and school gardens. Another shows the ration system: ration cards, and tapioca and sweet potato instead of rice. A key says different people had different experiences.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about a wartime occupation, and some learners have lived through war, conflict or displacement. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in the sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and let any learner step out without giving a reason. The lesson needs no violent images. The occupation also brought killings and harsh punishments; the lesson does not describe them and you do not need to. If learners raise them, say plainly that many people were harmed, then return to the sources. Preview before sharing: the NLB article mentions a harsh punishment in one line, and the video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners describe two different changes in daily life, one about school and one about food, with a source for each, without claiming everyone lived the same way. Evidence move: compare the MOE Heritage Centre's school rules with Lee Geok Boi's food history, then point to the photo's date, 2025, before learners say what it shows. A sound answer gives two different everyday effects backed by sources. Misconceptions to address: "all children attended normal classes", "everyone ate the same food", and the idea that the occupation automatically led to independence later.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the MOE page records rules and examples, not every school. The NLB article draws on the National Archives' oral history interviews (its first Japanese Occupation project, 1981–1985, recorded 179 people); memories are valuable but are one person's account, told decades later. The lesson leaves out the article's ration amounts and prices on purpose. The photo shows the restored building in 2025 with modern flats behind it. If you can get a licensed photo of a wartime ration card with clear provenance, it would make a stronger second picture.
